title: I spent the night in Cleveland's haunted Franklin Castle — here's what happened
excerpt: From a tour with the property's historian to a once-in-a-lifetime ghost-hunting investigation, here's what it's like to stay in the Franklin Castle.
content:
"Is anyone here with us?"

That's the question paranormal expert Steve Gonsalves, star of "Ghost Hunters" and "Ghost Nation," poses as my haunt-hunting group joins him inside the famously haunted Franklin Castle in Cleveland, Ohio. 

Almost on cue, a sharp beep pierces the silence: Our REM-POD has activated. The popular ghost-hunting gadget, with its telescopic antenna and radiating electromagnetic field, only alerts when something—or someone—crosses into its space.

A Dream (or Nightmare) Come True

I've always loved everything Halloween: haunted houses, ghost stories whispered around a fire, and anything that makes me question what lurks beyond the veil. 

But last October, my wildest dreams (or perhaps nightmares?) came true. 

I not only joined an investigative tour of Franklin Castle, but also met the castle's historian, traded ghost stories around a fire with s'mores and Cutwater cocktails, and spent the night inside the sprawling Queen Anne–style mansion, built in 1881 and brimming with eerie legends. 

Real Spirits Inside

Cutwater Spirits, the No. 1 spirits-based cocktail brand in the U.S., hosted a Halloween-themed campaign called "Real Spirits Inside." The name is a double entendre—celebrating both the premium quality of its canned cocktails (like the espresso martini with vodka I sipped throughout the spooktacular evening) and the ghosts that seemed to be activating our equipment inside Franklin Castle.

I brought my fellow spooky season-loving friend Emmy—who made sure to pack her holy water—for the adventure. We stayed the night before the sweepstakes winners arrived and previewed their spooky Franklin Castle itinerary. From the sounds of it, they also experienced plenty of paranormal activity, like doors creaking open in the middle of the night. (Here's a fun documentary-style video that details their stay.)

The Castle's Dark History

My own experience inside Franklin Castle was equal parts eerie and enchanting. Between the hidden passageways, the rumors of people being pushed on the staircase, and the occasional unexplained sounds echoing through the halls, I found myself torn between scientific curiosity and pure goosebumps.

The castle was built in 1881 by Hannes Tiedemann, a German immigrant and grocer-turned-banker, and his wife Louise. We learned from William G. Krejci, Franklin Castle's resident historian (and former resident himself), how proud Tiedemann was of his home—yet how his name became tangled in dark rumors. Tragically, several of his family members died in quick succession, including his 15-year-old daughter Emma, his mother, and three infants, all of whom are believed to haunt the house.

The mansion's haunted reputation became more public in the 1960s, when the Romano family bought it with plans to turn it into a restaurant. But on move-in day, two of their children came downstairs asking for a cookie for their new friend—a little girl dressed in all white. Mrs. Romano later saw a woman in a black gown standing in the turret on the third floor—the same room I was staying in. The family promptly moved out.

Shaken (and Stirred) Spirits

Before our ghost hunt, we joined a mixology session with artist and author Nikk Alcaraz, who showed us how to spin chocolate syrup spiderwebs atop espresso martinis and paint our glasses with tiny ghost designs made from marshmallow fluff. (Perfect tricks for any Halloween party.)

According to a new survey commissioned by Cutwater, more people believe in ghosts (44%) than believe canned cocktails are "real" cocktails (36%)—clearly, there's some myth-busting to do.

Into the Night

As we began our investigation, knowing the castle's history shaped our questions. We asked if the spirits still enjoy hosting guests or perhaps remembered the grand parties that once filled these halls. Admittedly, we were trying to appeal to their egos rather than stir up trauma.

From one of the castle's turrets, I could see a steady stream of people passing below—modern-day ghost tourists gazing up at the stately mansion, its pointed towers and iron gates silhouetted against the night sky.

I've always been a bit of a skeptic. Maybe that's what makes ghost hunting so fun: I'm not too scared, so I can lean in a little closer. Throughout my stay, we heard doors shutting, floors creaking, and my friend swore she felt the presence of Emma, the young girl who shares her name.

A Final Sign

My favorite moment came late that night when we returned to our guest quarters—a floor that had supposedly been closed off while we were eating dinner downstairs—and noticed something new: a shattered glass on the floor, spotted by Emmy. No one else had been in the room since we left it.

I'll take that as a resounding yes to the question of whether the spirits still love to entertain.
